title: Same Verb, Different Particle
intro: Get, take, make, put — the exact confusion that makes phrasal verbs feel like chaos instead of pattern. One base verb, wildly different meanings.

A2.why: “Up” means rising: you wake up, then you get up and have breakfast.

A2.right: enter a bus, train or plane
A2.why: You get on a bus, train or plane; for a car or taxi say “get in”.

A2.right: leave a bus, train or plane
A2.why: “Off” means away from: you get off the bus at your stop.
“Off” the ground: the plane takes off from Manises airport.
“Away” means removal: the waiter takes away your plates. Food “to take away” is “para llevar”.
You put on a coat or shoes: Spanish “ponerse”.

A2.right: return something to its proper place
A2.why: “Away” means to its place: put the shopping away in the cupboard.
Make up a story: invent it, Spanish “inventarse”.
Small vehicles you sit inside: get in a car, but get on a bus.

A2.right: take someone to a restaurant or the cinema
A2.why: He took his wife out for dinner in El Carmen: he invited her.
Firefighters put out the fire: Spanish “apagar”.

A2.right: return from a trip or holiday
A2.why: We got back from the Pyrenees late on Sunday: we returned from our trip.

B1.right: manage with the little you have
B1.why: With little money or little English, you can still get by: you just manage.

B1.right: recover from an illness or shock
B1.why: You climb over the problem: you recover from an illness or a shock.
He took up golf when he retired: he started a new hobby.
She takes after her mother: she looks or acts like her. Spanish “salir a”.
The shoes were too small, so I took them back: I returned them to the shop.
The old friends get together every Christmas: they meet up and spend time together.
Don't put off going to the doctor: don't postpone it.
She put forward a proposal at the meeting: she suggested it.

B1.right: escape from a place or person
B1.why: The outlaws got away before the sheriff arrived: they escaped.

B1.right: write notes of what someone says
B1.why: The nurse took down the patient's details: she wrote them on a form.

B1.right: give someone a bed for the night
B1.why: Friends put us up in Valencia during the Fallas: we stayed at their flat.

B1.right: have a good relationship with someone
B1.why: “I get on well with my sister-in-law”: we have a friendly relationship.

B2.why: You get through a hard week or an exam: you reach the end successfully.
A good teacher gets the idea across: the message reaches the listener.
Two meanings: take in information (understand it), or be taken in by a con man (deceived).
“I take it back”: you withdraw what you said, “retirar lo dicho”.

B2.right: compensate for a loss or mistake
B2.why: Extra hours make up for lost time: they compensate for it.

B2.right: steal and run away with something
B2.why: The thief made off with the cash box: he stole it and ran.
Spanish “aguantar”: I can't put up with the neighbours' dog any longer.
Put down your name on the list (write it), or put someone down (make them feel small).

B2.right: finally find time to do something
B2.why: I never get round to fixing the gate: I keep not finding the time.

B2.right: take control of a company or place
B2.why: When the founder retired, his daughter took over the business.

B2.right: transfer a caller to another person
B2.why: “I'll put you through to the doctor”: the receptionist connects your call.
After coffee, let's get down to business: start the real work.

C1.right: circumvent a rule, or travel to many places
C1.why: Get around a rule (find a way round it), or get around (travel a lot).

C1.right: imply something indirectly, or criticise persistently
C1.why: “What are you getting at?” = what do you mean? It can also mean to criticise repeatedly.

C1.right: start liking someone or something quickly
C1.why: She took to Valencia immediately: she liked it straight away.

C1.right: accept a responsibility, or hire someone
C1.why: Take on a challenge or new staff: accept a responsibility, or hire someone.

C1.right: manage with what's available, though not ideal
C1.why: With no doctor in town, the settlers made do with home remedies: not ideal, but enough.

C1.right: form an opinion or interpretation about something
C1.why: “What do you make of the new mayor?” = what's your opinion of him?

C1.right: communicate an idea clearly and convincingly
C1.why: A good speaker puts across an argument clearly and persuasively.

C1.right: attribute something to a particular cause
C1.why: He put his good health down to the Mediterranean diet: he said it was the cause.
Usually passive: “I was taken aback by his rudeness” = surprised and a little shocked.
Before he died, the rancher made the land over to his daughter.
She put in for a transfer to the Valencia office: she applied officially.
He got off with a fine instead of prison: get off = escape the heavy punishment you expected.
